I agree with what others are saying about companies being unwilling to take risks content and title-wise, but I think another big contributor to this is how much game companies are relying on hype.

Decades ago, it was far more likely that you’d discover a game after it was already finished and released, either through stumbling across it on your own or picking it up after watching somebody else play it. Either way, you’d be judging it for what it was right from the start. If you knew about it prior to that, you probably just knew that it was in the works and not much else.

But now instead of sticking with that risky “make something, advertise it, and see if it catches on” strategy, more companies seem to be relying on hyping up a big title before it’s even remotely finished, and banking on pre-orders and release day sales. Which, to be fair, makes sense for them as a business. If people are willing to consistently fork over $60+ for a currently nonexistent thing, why not?

Unfortunately, the problem with that strategy is that for the consumers, it guarantees a whole lot of disappointment because things are rarely as good as we imagine them to be. And instead of wandering blindly into games and judging them on their own merits, we’re judging them against our months of imagined expectations. No wonder everything seems shitty.

The worst part is that as long as people continue to be naive or want to get in on the Next Big Thing on the very first day, overhyping games will continue to be profitable for the companies. And when you combine that with the existence of DLC and the fact that it’s now the norm for games to receive constant updates, there’s no incentive for anybody to actually release a finished game, ever. I don’t know what the answer is here, really. I just know I’ve kind of given up and decided to pursue retro gaming instead.
